questions.qtext: Which of the following four languages is different from the other three?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

$\color{red}{\text{Detailed Video Solution:}}$ https://youtu.be/XF2ygVBjlTg?t=125

The language $\emptyset$ is empty, which means that it contains no words. All other languages are equal to $\{\lambda\}$. If you concatenate zero words from the empty language, you get the empty word. If you concatenate zero or more times the empty word, it will still be the empty word.

Correct Answer: A

questions.qtext: Which of the following four languages is different from the other three?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

$\color{red}{\text{Detailed Video Solution:}}$ https://youtu.be/XF2ygVBjlTg?t=596

The languages $(\{a, b\})^*,(\{b, a, a\})^*$, and $(\{a\} \cup\{b\})^*$ basically all state: choose either $a$ or $b$ and do that as often as you want. This gives all words over the alphabet $\{a, b\}$. The language $\left(\{a\}^* \cup\{b\}^*\right)$, however, states: take any amount of $a$'s or any amount of $b$'s. In particular this last language doesn't contain words like $a b$ that contain $a$'s and $b$'s.

Regular expression for $(\{a, b\})^*,(\{b, a, a\})^*$, and $(\{a\} \cup\{b\})^*$ is $(a+b)^*$

Regular expression for $\left(\{a\}^* \cup\{b\}^*\right)$ is $a^* + b^*$

Correct Answer: C

questions.qtext: Is there for all non-deterministic finite automata a deterministic finite automaton that recognizes the same language?

options.text: Yes, you can construct such an automaton using the power set construction.
Yes, because you are not required to have non-determinism in a nondeterministic automaton.
No, because in a non-deterministic automaton $\lambda$ transitions are allowed.
No, because non-deterministic automata are more efficient than deterministic automata.

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

$\color{red}{\text{Detailed Video Solution:}}$ https://youtu.be/XF2ygVBjlTg?t=1178

The second option makes no sense because this only explains that some NFAs are in fact already DFAs, but it doesn't explain why the other NFAs have an equivalent DFA.

The third and fourth options make no sense because the answer is 'yes'.

Correct Answer: A

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Option A: CORRECT, Every DFA is a NFA, but every NFA is a DFA that can be done by Power set construction. Because the DFA states consist of sets of NFA states, an n-state NFA may be converted to a DFA with at most $2^{n}$ states.

Options B,C: WRONG, we have the power of non-determinism and λ transition in a NFA.

Option D: Wrong, Every regular language is recognized by DFA and we know for every DFA NFA exists then we can say the regular language is also recognized by NFA , so NFA and DFA are equally efficient.

questions.qtext:
Let $\text{M}$ be a DFA. Say strings $x$ and $y$ in $\Sigma^*$ are indistinguishable, written $x \equiv y$ if and only if
$$
\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)
$$
Which of the following is/are necessarily true?

options.text: Every pair of strings in $\text{L(M)}$ are indistinguishable.
Two different strings in $\mathrm{L}(\mathrm{M})$ are never indistinguishable.
Indistinguishable relation on strings in $\Sigma^*$ is an equivalence relation.
Indistinguishable relation on strings in $\Sigma^*$ is a partial order relation.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 10)

Detailed Video Solution, with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/ldychl4M6fE?t=80

Since $\delta^*()$ is a function, the following hold
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text {Reflexive } & \delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right) \\
\text {Symmetric } & \left(\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)\right) \Rightarrow\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)\right) \\
\text {Transitive } & \left(\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)\right) \wedge\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, z\right)\right)\right) \Rightarrow\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, z\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
Therefore, indistinguishable is an equivalence relation on strings.

Basically, two strings are indistinguishable if, starting from the initial state, both strings lead to the same state.

Option $A$ is not correct. Conside this DFA $\text{M}$ as a counter example:

Strings $aa$ and $bb$ are in $\text{L(M)}$ but both are not indistinguishable because both strings end up in the different states.

Option $B$ is not correct. Strings $aa$ and $aaa$ are in $\text{L(M)}$ but both are indistinguishable because both strings end up in the same state.

Option $D$ is not correct because indistinguishable relation is not antisymmetric. This doesn't fullfil requirement for a relation to be partial order.

OptionB is wrong , because L(M) contains strings which are equivalent always

Option C is correct, by myhill nerode theorem

Option D is wrong, because they dont follow antisymmetricity

questions.qtext:
Let $M$ be a DFA. Say strings $x$ and $y$ in $\Sigma^*$ are indistinguishable, written $x \equiv y$ if and only if
$$
\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)
$$
Which of the following is/are necessarily true?

options.text: If strings $x, y$ are indistinguishable then $x a, ya$ are also indistinguishable, for every alphabet symbol $a.$
If strings $x a, y a$ are indistinguishable then $x, y$ are also indistinguishable, where a is an alphabet symbol.
If strings $x, y$ are indistinguishable then $x w, y w$ are also indistinguishable, for all strings $w$.
If strings $xw, yw$ are indistinguishable then $x, y$ are also indistinguishable, where $w$ is a string.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, C

Source solution 1 (score: 8)

Detailed Video Solution, with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/ldychl4M6fE?t=2359

Since $\delta^*()$ is a function, the following hold
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Reflexive } & \delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right) \\
\text { Symmetric } & \left(\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)\right) \Rightarrow\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)\right) \\
\text { Transitive } & \left(\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)\right) \wedge\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, y\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, z\right)\right)\right) \Rightarrow\left(\delta^*\left(q_0, x\right)=\delta^*\left(q_0, z\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
Therefore, indistinguishable is an equivalence relation on strings.

NOTE:
If strings $x, y$ are indistinguishable then $xw, yw$ are also indistinguishable, for all strings $w$.

Easy to prove, by definition $\&$ properties of a DFA.

Source solution 2 (score: 1)
δ*(q0​,x)=δ*(q0​,y) - this means that after reading the complete string x,y from the start state q0, the DFA ends in the same state.

A. If strings x,y are indistinguishable then xa,ya are also indistinguishable, for every alphabet symbol a. So, True.

This means x,y end on the same state so any transition on same symbol from there will lead to same next state.

B.If strings xa,ya are indistinguishable then x,y are also indistinguishable, where a is an alphabet symbol.

This means they land on the same state after reading the same symbol, but it is not necessary they take the same path before that so here x,y need not be indistinguishable if xa,ya are. Ex - δ*(q0,x)=P, δ*(q0,y)=Q, but δ*(q0,xa)=Z, and δ*(q0,ya)=Z.So, False.

C.If strings x,y are indistinguishable then xw,yw are also indistinguishable, for all strings w.

Same reasoning as A but with a string w. So True.

D. If strings xw,yw are indistinguishable then x,y are also indistinguishable, where w is a string.

Same reasoning as B but with a string. So False.

Answer - A,C

questions.qtext: If for a language $\text{L}$ is given that $\text{L}^*=\text{L},$ what does not necessarily follow?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 14)

Detailed Video Solution, with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/ldychl4M6fE?t=4605

If $\text{L}=\{\lambda\}$, then $\text{L}^*=\text{L}$. So the assumption that $\text{L}^*=\text{L}$ does not imply that $\text{L}$ is infinite.

Statement $\text{LL}=\text{L}$ holds, because if $w \in \text{LL},$ then $w=w_1 w_2 \in L^*=\text{L}$, and if $w \in \text{L},$ then $w=w \lambda \in \text{LL},$ because by definition $\lambda \in \text{L}^*$ and hence $\lambda \in \text{L}$.

Statement $\lambda \in \text{L}$ holds, because by definition $\lambda \in \text{L}^*,$ and hence $\lambda \in \text{L}$.

Statement $\text{L}$ is non-empty holds, because if $\text{L}=\emptyset$, then $\text{L}^*=\{\lambda\}$ which contradicts $\text{L}^*=\text{L}$.

Correct Answer: C

questions.qtext: If for a language $\text{L}$ is given that $\text{L}^\text{R}=\text{L},$ what does necessarily follow?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 30)
Statement 'if $w \in \text{L}^*$ then also $w^\text{R} \in \text{L}^*$' holds. Let $w \in \text{L}^*$. Then there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $w=w_1 \cdots w_k$ and $w_i \in \text{L}$ for $i \in\{1, \ldots, k\}$. Note that $w^\text{R}=\left(w_1 \cdots w_k\right)^\text{R}=w_k^\text{R} \cdots w_1^\text{R}$. However, because $\text{L}^\text{R}=\text{L}$, we have that $w_i^\text{R} \in \text{L}$ for $i \in\{1, \ldots, k\}$. Hence $w^\text{R}=w_k^\text{R} \cdots w_1^\text{R} \in \text{L}^*$.

Statement 'there is a $w \in \text{L}$ for which also $w^\text{R} \in \text{L}$ ' does not hold. Take $\text{L}=\emptyset$. Then $\text{L}^\text{R}=\emptyset=\text{L}$. However, there is no $w \in \text{L}$, so certainly no $w \in \text{L}$ for which $w^\text{R} \in \text{L}$.

Statement ' $\lambda \in \text{L}$, because $\lambda^\text{R}=\lambda$ ' does not hold. Take $\text{L}=\{a\}$. Then $\text{L}^\text{R}=\text{L}$, but $\lambda \notin \text{L}$.

Statement 'there is a $w \in \text{L}$ with $w^\text{R}=w$ ' does not hold. Take $\text{L}=$ $\{a b, b a\}$. Then $\text{L}^\text{R}=\text{L}$, but $(a b)^\text{R}=b a \neq a b$ and $(b a)^\text{R}=a b \neq b a$.

Correct Answer: A

questions.qtext: Which of the following regular expressions describes a language different from the others?
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 3)
Note that
$$
\mathcal{L}\left((a \cup b)^*\right)=\mathcal{L}\left(\left(a^* b^*\right)^*\right)=\mathcal{L}\left(\left(b^* a^*\right)^*\right)=\{a, b\}^*
$$
and that
$$
\mathcal{L}\left(a^* \cup b^*\right)=\{a\}^* \cup\{b\}^*
$$
So in particular $a b \notin\{a\}^* \cup\{b\}^*$, but $a b \in\{a, b\}^*$.

Correct Answer: D

questions.qtext: Which of the following regular expressions describes a language different from the others?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 5)
Note that
$$
\mathcal{L}\left(a^* b^*\right)=\mathcal{L}\left((a \cup a a)^*(b \cup b b)^*\right)=\mathcal{L}\left((\lambda \cup a)^*(\lambda \cup b)^*\right)=\left\{a^n b^m \mid n, m \in \mathbb{N}\right\}
$$
and that
$$
\mathcal{L}\left((\lambda \cup a a)^*(\lambda \cup b b)^*\right)=\left\{a^{2 n} b^{2 m} \mid n, m \in \mathbb{N}\right\}
$$
So in particular $a b \notin\left\{a^{2 n} b^{2 m} \mid n, m \in \mathbb{N}\right\}$, but $a b \in\left\{a^n b^m \mid n, m \in \mathbb{N}\right\}$.

Correct Answer: B

Just check we can make $ab$ in every regular expression but can’t make it from $2^{nd}$ regular expression that’s why it is different from others.
